title: Plan
hook: A generator transfer card sits untouched until the hurricane drill finds the missing role.
counterintuition: Planning is not a promise that reality will obey but a shared base that lets people adapt when the original route breaks.
tryThisNow: Before your next handoff, say the aim and first step. Add the likely failure and the backup move.
keyTakeaway: A good plan gives people intent and roles plus checks and contingencies, so pressure can change the route without breaking the mission.

breakdown.fastRead:
A generator transfer card sits untouched until the hurricane drill finds the missing role.. The team wants the simple story: planning removes uncertainty. That story is too small for the pressure in front of them.

The move is to prepare intent, roles, checks, and backups before pressure changes the route. It gives people a visible standard, not just a feeling about leadership. When the leader changes contingency, the next action becomes easier to see and harder to dodge.

Planning earns its keep when the original route breaks.
breakdown.deepRead:
Planning raises adaptability when people share commander’s intent, rehearse roles, and think through contingencies before pressure arrives.

A leader can miss this by reaching for the nearest emotional answer. Get louder. Sound tougher. Name the weak performer. Those moves may feel decisive, but they leave contingency untouched. The useful question is what the team has been taught to do by the current signals, checks, and habits.

Intent tells people what must survive when the steps have to change.

Look at the planned pressure point for Plan: shared aim, practice, and fallback thinking. The pressure is the place where the principle has to work while people are tired, proud, rushed, or uncertain. The leader does not need a perfect room. The leader needs a clearer next move.

There is a limit in Plan. Contingency does not cancel personal responsibility, judgment, or hard correction. It sets the order: make the condition visible first, then correct the person or tactic inside that clearer standard.

A second pass makes contingency practical. The leader points to the visible cue, has one person repeat the next action, and names the check that will prove whether the team understood. That small rehearsal turns contingency from a line in the room into behavior people can carry when the leader is not standing beside them.
breakdown.fullRead:
The deeper test arrives when the first fix feels satisfying. A team can nod at contingency, run one clean meeting, and still return to the old pattern next week. Real repair changes what people see, repeat, and check when pressure returns.

For Plan, ask it in operational terms: if the group met the same pressure tomorrow, how would contingency make the right action easier? The answer might be a cue, a route, an owner, a handoff, or a practiced fallback. If nothing visible changes, the lesson has not reached the work.

shared aim, practice, and fallback thinking matters because it prevents the idea from becoming soft advice. The pressure is specific. The leader is not polishing a slogan. The leader is changing how people act when the outcome can still be lost. That means contingency has to show up in a visible procedure, spoken intent, repeated standard, or decision rule.

The objection changes shape here: commander’s intent does not mean talent and effort are irrelevant. Weak effort still needs correction. Low skill still needs training. The leader gets a cleaner truth by inspecting the controlled condition first. If contingency was clear and ignored, correction lands on firmer ground. If it was vague, the first repair is obvious.

The final discipline is restraint. Do not turn the principle into a universal hammer. Use it to see the next controllable part of the mission. Then act there. A rehearsal is a cheap place to find an expensive miss.

The strongest version of this move also changes the next review. Instead of asking whether people tried hard, the leader asks whether contingency was visible enough to guide a tired person under pressure. If it was not, the repair belongs in the environment: a clearer handoff, a shorter cue, a sharper owner, or a rehearsal before the stakes rise. If it was visible and still ignored, correction can be direct because the standard was real. That order matters. It keeps leadership from becoming blame first, and it keeps accountability from turning into a speech. rehearse roles and backup moves only counts when the next person can see what to do differently.

A final check for Plan is whether contingency survives when the leader leaves the room. The best repair leaves a mark people can use: a line on the board, a repeated phrase, a changed checklist, a clearer owner, or a rehearsed stop point. Without that mark, the team has to rebuild the lesson from memory every time pressure returns. With it, the lesson becomes part of the work. The leader can then spend attention on judgment instead of re-explaining the basics. That is the practical payoff: less drama around the repeat problem and more room to handle the new problem honestly.

reviewCards.front: A team is drifting around contingency. What should you retrieve first?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the planned move in plain form: prepare intent, roles, checks, and backups before pressure changes the route. Start with a visible action, not a mood or slogan.

reviewCards.front: The tempting answer is planning removes uncertainty. What question breaks that reflex?
reviewCards.back: Ask which leadership-controlled condition is shaping the result right now. That question points to the next repair instead of the easiest story.

reviewCards.front: A person near the problem made a mistake. How does the leader keep the review useful?
reviewCards.back: Handle the person inside the standard, but first inspect the signal, role, check, or purpose the leader controlled.

reviewCards.front: The room wants a fast answer. What makes the answer strong enough to use?
reviewCards.back: It changes what people will do on the next pass. A strong answer leaves a clearer cue, owner, route, or standard behind.

reviewCards.front: You fixed one visible symptom. What proves the principle reached the work?
reviewCards.back: The next team can repeat the right action without fresh heroics from you. The environment, standard, or communication now carries part of the load.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice using contingency as an operational tool. The skill is to prepare intent, roles, checks, and backups before pressure changes the route before the team settles into the easy story.

ifThenPlans.plan: If the review circles blame, then name the contingency condition first and assign the next visible repair.
If a handoff feels fragile, then state the owner, standard, and check that will carry contingency into the next shift.
If someone repeats a mistake, then inspect whether contingency was taught, modeled, and checked before adding correction.
If your own system slips, then change one cue or rule so contingency is easier next time.
